Loadshedding Collateral Damage

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The South African economy is buckling under the stress of load shedding. At the flick of a switch, Eskom is putting the lives and livelihoods of ordinary citizens at risk.

Unique Selling Point:
What is the cost of load shedding?

In terms of rands and cents, the industry rule of thumb is that the loss to the South African economy is the cost of producing the power, that has been shed from the system, multiplied by 7.

In reality, the cost to South Africans of load shedding is far reaching and deep - business are lost and lives are ruined - and for Eskom it’s as easy as flicking a switch on and off … or is it?

We try to live by the load shedding schedule – but more often than not a two and a half hour outage disrupts our lives for much longer. Increasingly on turning the power back on substations trip, Eskom, industrial and domestic equipment blow. The consequences to some South Africans are more catastrophic. Unreliable electricity supply can lead to unreliable supply of life-saving oxygen, power surges can electrocute and kill in the home. And in the economy at large fragile electricity supply can cut off much needed investment.

Summary:
As we try to live our lives according to Eskom’s load shedding schedule, the dire state of South Africa’s power utility is evident all around the country. I propose we put out a call for viewer submissions of photos/videos of electricity infrastructure in their neighbourhoods – open electricity boxes on the streets, weird cables, substations and how people are living during load shedding events. Nationwide submissions bring home the fact that all South Africans are affected and on the back of the recent Pothole Pandemic story viewers can see that their submissions are valuable to the show.

We will visit case studies to go deeper into some of the stories of electric disruption. Like Zarina Loonat from Azaadville, Krugersdorp whose elderly mother is reliant on oxygen to survive, and Jean van Vollenstee from Ekurhuleni whose son, who has asthma, could not use his nebulizer at home during load shedding and had to be rushed to hospital.

To get at the structural crisis we interview Mike Rossouw, an electrical engineer and past Eskom troubleshooter, to investigate the reasons behind load shedding and the damage caused materially by power outages and surges. I have also requested an interview with André de Ruyter for Eskom’s side of the story (which Russouw has an experienced take on).

Concerning the effect of load shedding on the economy we interview economist Khaya Sithole, with reference to inter-linkages between multidimensional poverty and electricity.

Further information:
Two and a half hour load shedding is generally not what it means. People leave their appliances on and overload the system. Distributors blow or substations trip. Eskom teams are continually going to the substations to fix problems caused by flicking the switch back on. When they get there the state of the substation can be even more messed up, as load shedding provides opportunities for thieves to steal cables. The complications caused by electricity reboot means power can be out for four or five hours at a time, three times a day – or in some areas even days and weeks.

So what is this actually doing to the infrastructure of substations and the way electricity is being utilised? Is the current load shedding schedule optimum from an engineering point of view? And what are the damages being created down the line?

A vicious cycle of load shedding is putting an enormous strain and stress on the distribution system. We are reducing the life of power plants, because they're now being pushed to the limit which puts a strain on maintenance. Maintenance itself is very constrained, because of all the load shedding. Eskom doesn't have much opportunity to take the load off on a planned basis to do the maintenance that is necessary. So the whole system is stacking up in terms of stresses and strains and pressures, costs, resources etc.
Mike Rossouw argues that at bare minimum there should be a gap of 12 hours between load shedding events of about 2 or 2 and a half hours maximum, to minimize material damage to Eskom's equipment, people's way of life and electrical appliances in general. He likens load shedding to turning off and on the engine of a car when it is in full flow driving along a highway.

All this pressure on the substations, the distributors and the maintenance, the compounding costs have been accumulating in the background. What started as rational load shedding for maintenance purposes in the early 2000s reached the surreal stage when Eskom claimed not to be load shedding, where in actuality breakdowns were reported by management as planned work, so load shedding did ensue under another guise and maintenance was postponed.

According to Rossouw, the planning at present is not up to scratch and to make matters worse, when Eskom do take a plant down, the quality of workmanship is not where it should be. And all this is aggravated by the fact that Eskom are seriously struggling with leadership, weak management and supervision. Problems that Rossouw says can be addressed, but would take at least five years even if tackled properly.

In the meantime Rossouw says he can furnish the calculation of the current cost of load shedding in Rands and cents and expand on the nature of the electricity producing business itself - the business of instantaneous production for instantaneous demand - and the prospect for renewable IPPs.

With the economy as it is, aggravated by COVID, the last thing we need is further damage from load shedding. Even though people say they can quantify it, the damage is much deeper. According to a current study using the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), if you don’t have reliable electricity it prevents investment. Who wants to invest in a country which has unreliable power supply? SA PLC (South Africa seen as a company) offers to make it extremely difficult to keep your business running seamlessly while draining your labour of energy. Lack of investment means less in the government coffers to bail out Eskom and to fund recovery. Might renewable energy grants be the only option for bailouts in the future?

Press Release:


There’s much more to load shedding than the lights going out. The collateral damage is making the lives of South Africans a misery.

Script:


VO: Load shedding // (beat lights go out) // - part of the South African landscape, on and off, since 2007.

Time lapse shot transition into link… from old story….

visual transitions to candle being lit
LINK: So how much longer are South Africans going to continue living in the dark? If Eskom goes on like this, there's nothing easy about the future we face

Customer: Please tell me why everytime there is load shedding, it takes so long to come back on? The other morning it took four hours.
City Power: Sometimes mám there is an overload when it's supposed to be restored, this is when you've got all your appliances left on during the load shedding.
Customer: The other night they told me the distributor was blown.
City Power: That is at the substation so it could be anything

VO: It feels like groundhog day, the same electricity shortages day in day out. In 2019, Eskom warned government the country was short of around 4000 megawatts of power, and since then not much has changed.
(Protest shots of Ekurhuleni residents.. )
More and more South Africans have had enough and are taking to the streets in protest. Ekurhuleni metro in Gauteng reflects the despair across the country.

Jean: You get told you'll go off at a certain time and come on at a certain time after three hours, but in our area, what happens is we come on at the set time, but within five minutes, the power goes off again and then we're off for round three days.
Bongani: Three days?
Jean: Three days just for a technician to flick a switch back on

VO: Jean van Vollenstee is an Ekurhuleni resident who lives in Primrose East, and he’s not the only angry rate payer. Just around the corner Elzette Pretorius, a single mom, works online from home, for an international company. She works mainly at night when load shedding is at its peak.

Elzette: I hate it. It frustrates me. And I keep thinking that it's another hour that I'm losing another bit of paycheck that I'm losing. Money that could have gone to my kids could have paid for bills. They will come out, they will switch it on, they won't wait to make sure that everything is stable and everybody is on and it will trip again and they've gone already.

Bongani: What's the longest you've been without power?
Jean: Five days, that week I lost an appliance and just recently I had to replace my microwave as well. When the power comes back there's a huge spike.

VO: So why does load shedding leave some people out of power for days and even weeks on end? Mike Rossouw, CEO of the energy users group, used to be a trouble shooter for Eskom.

Mike Rossouw: The reason is that there are so many pieces of componentry within every power station unit in Eskom that at the moment is in a situation where it could fail at any moment in time. There are so many of them that need a complete overhaul. And because there's a problem in planning, when they open up a machine, they discover defects that they didn't know about.
Bongani: Broadly speaking, how bad is the state of Eskom's infrastructure?
Mike Rossouw: Today the infrastructure, particularly in generation, is probably worse than it's ever been.

VO: Sikonathi Mantshantsha, spokesperson for Eskom, admits the picture looks bleak.

Sikonathi Mantshantsha: The truth is, this infrastructure was not designed to be switched on and off as it happens. Sometimes when the power is restored, the breaker does not close and some things get damaged.

VO: Due to flawed design and construction, the Medupi and Kusile power plants have taken much of the blame for failing to address the shortfall in electricity supply, but at the same time existing plants have deteriorated because of load shedding and trying to keep the lights on - at the expense of much needed maintenance.

Mike Rossouw: So the load shedding today is predominantly poor performance of the generation fleet, even the new plant.

Sikonathi Mantshantsha: The reality though is load shedding is exactly the best way to avoid calamity. And it is the one thing that South Africa has standing between it and a blackout.

VO: The unpredictability of load shedding and its repercussions is putting severe strain on households like Elzette’s.

Bongani: What's the biggest amount you've lost because of this?
Elzette: Almost 4000 Rand.
Bongani: In a single month?
Elzette: In a single month? Yes.

Bongani: People might be able to accept the reality of load shedding. I could pick up my phone and get an SMS that says power is going to be cut off in an hour.
Sikonathi Mantshantsha: South Africa does not have at this point the ability to store power. So you have to use what you have. Eskom is now at this very point able to supply just over 33,000 megawatts of electricity, which is still not enough in the winter.
Bongani: So every time the lights go off, we're in a crisis?
Sikonathi Mantshantsha: We have been in a crisis for at least 13 years now. That's our reality.

VO: To cap it all, criminals go out on the prowl during load shedding. Ekurhuleni community activist Deon Graaf, has taken it upon himself to keep vigilance over local substations.

Deon: A lot of the substations in the area is outdated and there's always a cable problem.

LINK: When there's load shedding a mini substation like this is an easy target for the cable thieves because they know there's no voltage coming through. And that's what led to this one catching fire.

Deon: So when they do steal the cables, obviously, it makes some kind of a short, and then it burns out. Then again, we sitting a few days without power. I try to keep a log of all the incidents in the area, so that we can, if they say no, but there wasn't a problem. We can show them, "but listen here. Here's the problem"

Sikonathi Mantshantsha: There are areas in Soweto that are four weeks without electricity, because the illegal connections overload the transformers and destroy them. When we say load shedding it is because Eskom itself is not able to meet the demand, but the localised issues can be attributed to, to either customers stealing the infrastructure through overloading with electricity and and you have other municipal problems where where the local distribution holder is not able to meet the demand.

VO: Eskom says it is doing what it can to assist municipalities, but this has not been the experience of Azaadville residents in Gauteng, who also endure prolonged power outages. Community member Zarina Loonat, fondly known as Aunty Za, is exasperated.

Zarina: Eskom refused to come, saying that it's a municipality problem. Municipality said well, they serve no purpose without Eskom, so they can't help us unless Eskom helps us and Eskom says they can't help us, it's a Mogale city problem. The water reservoir there is no generator on that motor, so obviously when there's no electricity, there's always a problem with water supply.

LINK: For families who are reliant on electricity for life support, oxygen, and other critical medical equipment, extended power outages can be catastrophic.

Zarina: I've come up in arms because my mum is a COPD patient, she lives 24/7 365 on oxygen, and now with this excessive load shedding, the inverter only lasts for four hours. She doesn't have electricity, nobody can give us answers and six hours later, she still doesn't have oxygen.

Jean: Two weeks ago on a Friday night, our son got an asthma attack and when he gets that we have to plug in the nebulizer. But that specific night we couldn't do it and I had to rush my son to hospital to the emergency department.


VO: And the cost of load shedding’s collateral damage to the South African economy is unquantifiable, argues analyst, Khaya Sithole

Khaya Sithole: There is indeed the risk that the people that need constant supply of electricity, whether it's the factories or whether it's the schools or every other part of the ecosystem, when they cannot be guaranteed uninterrupted power supply, it does call upon them to start doing things a bit differently. So the costs of that are incremental.


VO: A recent international report tracked the lack of electricity globally and its effect on multidimensional poverty, which impacts three key aspects, health, education and living standards.

Khaya Sithole: This data predates the covid 19 pandemic. So as you've seen, over the past year, when a lot of educational institutions have then said, let us migrate to online platforms, you can imagine what that has meant for people whose access to the electricity grid is compromised historically, and presently. So it is indeed multidimensional in nature, the effects of just lacking proper access to electricity are going to affect people not just now, but for generations to come.
Bongani: So how much further would this economy be if we could guarantee stable electricity?
Khaya Sithole: Whoever says I want to come and do something, they will definitely ask about the question of the stability of the electricity supply, and for some people that will indeed become the deal breaker. They do that assessment and then they come to the conclusion that we're not a viable investment destination.

VO: According to Eskom, government is in the process of addressing the country's dire energy shortage, and now private operators will be able to generate up to 100 megawatts of electricity without a licence.

Sikhonathi Mantshantsha: Earlier this year, they made the announcement that the government will procure 3600 megawatts of generation capacity that will come in about 18 months to help ease these constraints.
Bongani: Are you able to estimate when the end will come?
Sikonathi Mantshantsha: For the foreseeable future load shedding will be part of daily life. South Africa has to install at least 4000 megawatts of new generation capacity before we can end that. For Eskom’s part, we really have to see successes in repairing the infrastructure. You will see a significant difference in the last quarter of this year. And that's not to eliminate load shedding,but significantly reduce it.

Press Release: There’s much more to load shedding than the lights going out. The collateral damage is making the lives of South Africans a misery. Script: VO: Load shedding // (beat lights go out) // - part of the South African landscape, on and off, since 2007. Time lapse shot transition into link… from old story…. visual transitions to candle being lit LINK: So how much longer are South Africans going to continue living in the dark? If Eskom goes on like this, there's nothing easy about the future we face Customer: Please tell me why everytime there is load shedding, it takes so long to come back on? The other morning it took four hours. City Power: Sometimes mám there is an overload when it's supposed to be restored, this is when you've got all your appliances left on during the load shedding. Customer: The other night they told me the distributor was blown. City Power: That is at the substation so it could be anything VO: It feels like groundhog day, the same electricity shortages day in day out. In 2019, Eskom warned government the country was short of around 4000 megawatts of power, and since then not much has changed. (Protest shots of Ekurhuleni residents.. ) More and more South Africans have had enough and are taking to the streets in protest. Ekurhuleni metro in Gauteng reflects the despair across the country. Jean: You get told you'll go off at a certain time and come on at a certain time after three hours, but in our area, what happens is we come on at the set time, but within five minutes, the power goes off again and then we're off for round three days. Bongani: Three days? Jean: Three days just for a technician to flick a switch back on VO: Jean van Vollenstee is an Ekurhuleni resident who lives in Primrose East, and he’s not the only angry rate payer. Just around the corner Elzette Pretorius, a single mom, works online from home, for an international company. She works mainly at night when load shedding is at its peak. Elzette: I hate it. It frustrates me. And I keep thinking that it's another hour that I'm losing another bit of paycheck that I'm losing. Money that could have gone to my kids could have paid for bills. They will come out, they will switch it on, they won't wait to make sure that everything is stable and everybody is on and it will trip again and they've gone already. Bongani: What's the longest you've been without power? Jean: Five days, that week I lost an appliance and just recently I had to replace my microwave as well. When the power comes back there's a huge spike. VO: So why does load shedding leave some people out of power for days and even weeks on end? Mike Rossouw, CEO of the energy users group, used to be a trouble shooter for Eskom. Mike Rossouw: The reason is that there are so many pieces of componentry within every power station unit in Eskom that at the moment is in a situation where it could fail at any moment in time. There are so many of them that need a complete overhaul. And because there's a problem in planning, when they open up a machine, they discover defects that they didn't know about. Bongani: Broadly speaking, how bad is the state of Eskom's infrastructure? Mike Rossouw: Today the infrastructure, particularly in generation, is probably worse than it's ever been. VO: Sikonathi Mantshantsha, spokesperson for Eskom, admits the picture looks bleak. Sikonathi Mantshantsha: The truth is, this infrastructure was not designed to be switched on and off as it happens. Sometimes when the power is restored, the breaker does not close and some things get damaged. VO: Due to flawed design and construction, the Medupi and Kusile power plants have taken much of the blame for failing to address the shortfall in electricity supply, but at the same time existing plants have deteriorated because of load shedding and trying to keep the lights on - at the expense of much needed maintenance. Mike Rossouw: So the load shedding today is predominantly poor performance of the generation fleet, even the new plant. Sikonathi Mantshantsha: The reality though is load shedding is exactly the best way to avoid calamity. And it is the one thing that South Africa has standing between it and a blackout. VO: The unpredictability of load shedding and its repercussions is putting severe strain on households like Elzette’s. Bongani: What's the biggest amount you've lost because of this? Elzette: Almost 4000 Rand. Bongani: In a single month? Elzette: In a single month? Yes. Bongani: People might be able to accept the reality of load shedding. I could pick up my phone and get an SMS that says power is going to be cut off in an hour. Sikonathi Mantshantsha: South Africa does not have at this point the ability to store power. So you have to use what you have. Eskom is now at this very point able to supply just over 33,000 megawatts of electricity, which is still not enough in the winter. Bongani: So every time the lights go off, we're in a crisis? Sikonathi Mantshantsha: We have been in a crisis for at least 13 years now. That's our reality. VO: To cap it all, criminals go out on the prowl during load shedding. Ekurhuleni community activist Deon Graaf, has taken it upon himself to keep vigilance over local substations. Deon: A lot of the substations in the area is outdated and there's always a cable problem. LINK: When there's load shedding a mini substation like this is an easy target for the cable thieves because they know there's no voltage coming through. And that's what led to this one catching fire. Deon: So when they do steal the cables, obviously, it makes some kind of a short, and then it burns out. Then again, we sitting a few days without power. I try to keep a log of all the incidents in the area, so that we can, if they say no, but there wasn't a problem. We can show them, "but listen here. Here's the problem" Sikonathi Mantshantsha: There are areas in Soweto that are four weeks without electricity, because the illegal connections overload the transformers and destroy them. When we say load shedding it is because Eskom itself is not able to meet the demand, but the localised issues can be attributed to, to either customers stealing the infrastructure through overloading with electricity and and you have other municipal problems where where the local distribution holder is not able to meet the demand. VO: Eskom says it is doing what it can to assist municipalities, but this has not been the experience of Azaadville residents in Gauteng, who also endure prolonged power outages. Community member Zarina Loonat, fondly known as Aunty Za, is exasperated. Zarina: Eskom refused to come, saying that it's a municipality problem. Municipality said well, they serve no purpose without Eskom, so they can't help us unless Eskom helps us and Eskom says they can't help us, it's a Mogale city problem. The water reservoir there is no generator on that motor, so obviously when there's no electricity, there's always a problem with water supply. LINK: For families who are reliant on electricity for life support, oxygen, and other critical medical equipment, extended power outages can be catastrophic. Zarina: I've come up in arms because my mum is a COPD patient, she lives 24/7 365 on oxygen, and now with this excessive load shedding, the inverter only lasts for four hours. She doesn't have electricity, nobody can give us answers and six hours later, she still doesn't have oxygen. Jean: Two weeks ago on a Friday night, our son got an asthma attack and when he gets that we have to plug in the nebulizer. But that specific night we couldn't do it and I had to rush my son to hospital to the emergency department. VO: And the cost of load shedding’s collateral damage to the South African economy is unquantifiable, argues analyst, Khaya Sithole Khaya Sithole: There is indeed the risk that the people that need constant supply of electricity, whether it's the factories or whether it's the schools or every other part of the ecosystem, when they cannot be guaranteed uninterrupted power supply, it does call upon them to start doing things a bit differently. So the costs of that are incremental. VO: A recent international report tracked the lack of electricity globally and its effect on multidimensional poverty, which impacts three key aspects, health, education and living standards. Khaya Sithole: This data predates the covid 19 pandemic. So as you've seen, over the past year, when a lot of educational institutions have then said, let us migrate to online platforms, you can imagine what that has meant for people whose access to the electricity grid is compromised historically, and presently. So it is indeed multidimensional in nature, the effects of just lacking proper access to electricity are going to affect people not just now, but for generations to come. Bongani: So how much further would this economy be if we could guarantee stable electricity? Khaya Sithole: Whoever says I want to come and do something, they will definitely ask about the question of the stability of the electricity supply, and for some people that will indeed become the deal breaker. They do that assessment and then they come to the conclusion that we're not a viable investment destination. VO: According to Eskom, government is in the process of addressing the country's dire energy shortage, and now private operators will be able to generate up to 100 megawatts of electricity without a licence. Sikhonathi Mantshantsha: Earlier this year, they made the announcement that the government will procure 3600 megawatts of generation capacity that will come in about 18 months to help ease these constraints. Bongani: Are you able to estimate when the end will come? Sikonathi Mantshantsha: For the foreseeable future load shedding will be part of daily life. South Africa has to install at least 4000 megawatts of new generation capacity before we can end that. For Eskom’s part, we really have to see successes in repairing the infrastructure. You will see a significant difference in the last quarter of this year. And that's not to eliminate load shedding,but significantly reduce it.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The South African economy is buckling under the stress of load shedding. At the flick of a switch, Eskom is putting the lives and livelihoods of ordinary citizens at risk.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: What is the cost of load shedding? In terms of rands and cents, the industry rule of thumb is that the loss to the South African economy is the cost of producing the power, that has been shed from the system, multiplied by 7. In reality, the cost to South Africans of load shedding is far reaching and deep - business are lost and lives are ruined - and for Eskom it’s as easy as flicking a switch on and off … or is it? We try to live by the load shedding schedule – but more often than not a two and a half hour outage disrupts our lives for much longer. Increasingly on turning the power back on substations trip, Eskom, industrial and domestic equipment blow. The consequences to some South Africans are more catastrophic. Unreliable electricity supply can lead to unreliable supply of life-saving oxygen, power surges can electrocute and kill in the home. And in the economy at large fragile electricity supply can cut off much needed investment.
metadata.Summary: As we try to live our lives according to Eskom’s load shedding schedule, the dire state of South Africa’s power utility is evident all around the country. I propose we put out a call for viewer submissions of photos/videos of electricity infrastructure in their neighbourhoods – open electricity boxes on the streets, weird cables, substations and how people are living during load shedding events. Nationwide submissions bring home the fact that all South Africans are affected and on the back of the recent Pothole Pandemic story viewers can see that their submissions are valuable to the show. We will visit case studies to go deeper into some of the stories of electric disruption. Like Zarina Loonat from Azaadville, Krugersdorp whose elderly mother is reliant on oxygen to survive, and Jean van Vollenstee from Ekurhuleni whose son, who has asthma, could not use his nebulizer at home during load shedding and had to be rushed to hospital. To get at the structural crisis we interview Mike Rossouw, an electrical engineer and past Eskom troubleshooter, to investigate the reasons behind load shedding and the damage caused materially by power outages and surges. I have also requested an interview with André de Ruyter for Eskom’s side of the story (which Russouw has an experienced take on). Concerning the effect of load shedding on the economy we interview economist Khaya Sithole, with reference to inter-linkages between multidimensional poverty and electricity.
metadata.Further information: Two and a half hour load shedding is generally not what it means. People leave their appliances on and overload the system. Distributors blow or substations trip. Eskom teams are continually going to the substations to fix problems caused by flicking the switch back on. When they get there the state of the substation can be even more messed up, as load shedding provides opportunities for thieves to steal cables. The complications caused by electricity reboot means power can be out for four or five hours at a time, three times a day – or in some areas even days and weeks. So what is this actually doing to the infrastructure of substations and the way electricity is being utilised? Is the current load shedding schedule optimum from an engineering point of view? And what are the damages being created down the line? A vicious cycle of load shedding is putting an enormous strain and stress on the distribution system. We are reducing the life of power plants, because they're now being pushed to the limit which puts a strain on maintenance. Maintenance itself is very constrained, because of all the load shedding. Eskom doesn't have much opportunity to take the load off on a planned basis to do the maintenance that is necessary. So the whole system is stacking up in terms of stresses and strains and pressures, costs, resources etc. Mike Rossouw argues that at bare minimum there should be a gap of 12 hours between load shedding events of about 2 or 2 and a half hours maximum, to minimize material damage to Eskom's equipment, people's way of life and electrical appliances in general. He likens load shedding to turning off and on the engine of a car when it is in full flow driving along a highway. All this pressure on the substations, the distributors and the maintenance, the compounding costs have been accumulating in the background. What started as rational load shedding for maintenance purposes in the early 2000s reached the surreal stage when Eskom claimed not to be load shedding, where in actuality breakdowns were reported by management as planned work, so load shedding did ensue under another guise and maintenance was postponed. According to Rossouw, the planning at present is not up to scratch and to make matters worse, when Eskom do take a plant down, the quality of workmanship is not where it should be. And all this is aggravated by the fact that Eskom are seriously struggling with leadership, weak management and supervision. Problems that Rossouw says can be addressed, but would take at least five years even if tackled properly. In the meantime Rossouw says he can furnish the calculation of the current cost of load shedding in Rands and cents and expand on the nature of the electricity producing business itself - the business of instantaneous production for instantaneous demand - and the prospect for renewable IPPs. With the economy as it is, aggravated by COVID, the last thing we need is further damage from load shedding. Even though people say they can quantify it, the damage is much deeper. According to a current study using the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), if you don’t have reliable electricity it prevents investment. Who wants to invest in a country which has unreliable power supply? SA PLC (South Africa seen as a company) offers to make it extremely difficult to keep your business running seamlessly while draining your labour of energy. Lack of investment means less in the government coffers to bail out Eskom and to fund recovery. Might renewable energy grants be the only option for bailouts in the future?
